subject: math

objective.text: Compare and sort polygons by sides, angles and parallel lines. Learn what a regular polygon is.

source_ref.section: Lesson objective

objective.recap_text: A polygon's side count gives its general group. Other clues help you choose more specific groups. Parallel sides, equal sides and right angles help classify quadrilaterals. Rectangle and rhombus groups overlap at squares. A regular polygon has equal sides and equal angles. Finer ruler marks help record smaller differences in length.

explanations.title: Parallel sides and quadrilateral groups
explanations.text: A quadrilateral has four straight sides. Parallel lines stay the same distance apart and do not meet. A trapezoid has at least one pair of opposite sides parallel. We use this meaning of trapezoid throughout this lesson. A parallelogram has two pairs of opposite sides parallel.

source_ref.section: Manual source clarification requested by Amna, 12 October 2026

explanations.reflection_prompt: How do parallel sides help you tell quadrilateral groups apart?
protected_statements: A trapezoid has at least one pair of opposite sides parallel.
A parallelogram has two pairs of opposite sides parallel.

explanations.title: Rectangle and rhombus groups overlap
explanations.text: A rectangle has four right angles. A right angle makes a square corner. A rhombus has four equal sides. A square has four equal sides and four right angles. It belongs to both the rectangle and rhombus groups. These groups overlap; their shared group is squares. A square is also a parallelogram, a trapezoid and a quadrilateral. Not every rectangle is a rhombus. Not every rhombus is a rectangle.

explanations.title: Regular polygons
explanations.text: A regular polygon has all equal sides and all equal angles. A square is a regular quadrilateral.

explanations.title: Side count gives a general group name
explanations.text: Side count gives a polygon its general group name. A six-sided polygon is a hexagon, even if its shape looks unusual. Four-sided polygons are quadrilaterals. Their other features can give them more specific names, such as rectangle or rhombus.

source_ref.section: Manual source clarification requested by Amna, 12 October 2026

explanations.title: Pick the most precise unit
explanations.text: On an inch ruler, quarter-inch marks are closer together than half-inch marks. These finer divisions let you record smaller differences in side length. For this comparison, use the quarter-inch marks. Do not assume the smallest unit is best for every measuring task.

examples.title: Using parallel-side clues
examples.text: A quadrilateral with two pairs of opposite sides parallel is a parallelogram. It also fits our trapezoid group because two pairs include at least one pair.

source_ref.section: Manual source clarification requested by Amna, 12 October 2026

examples.title: A square belongs to overlapping groups
examples.text: A square has four equal sides and four right angles. The equal sides place it in the rhombus group. The right angles place it in the rectangle group. A rectangle whose sides are not all equal is not a rhombus.

source_ref.section: Manual source clarification requested by Amna, 12 October 2026

examples.title: An unusual hexagon
examples.text: A regular hexagon and an unusual-looking hexagon both have six sides. Both belong to the hexagon group. Their shapes can look different.

source_ref.section: Manual source clarification requested by Amna, 12 October 2026

examples.title: Comparing ruler divisions
examples.text: Look between inch marks on the ruler. Half-inch marks divide that space into larger steps than quarter-inch marks. The quarter-inch marks let you describe a smaller difference in side length.
